set.name: ZOI
set.hook: Tasting menus on a top-floor terrace in the palace's south wall, looking straight over the Riva and the port.
set.why: The dining room is built into the southern façade of Diocletian's Palace, and the terrace sits on the top floor above the Riva, so the view runs from the palm promenade to the ferries and the islands. The house opened in 2017 and has kept a MICHELIN recommendation since. In 2026 the kitchen belongs to Alberto García Pérez, who trained at Aponiente and Martín Berasategui, and the cooking reads as Mediterranean, built on the technique of those two Spanish kitchens.
set.verdict: The most complete grand dinner in the city centre, and the one Gault&Millau ranks highest of these three at 17/20. You pay for the terrace as much as the plates, and the price sits in MICHELIN's top bracket. Book the terrace, take the tasting menu, and confirm it is trading before you promise it to guests in November.
set.signature: The tasting menu on the top-floor terrace
set.caveat: Dinner only; winter schedule not published, call before promising it after October; online booking not via MICHELIN

set.hook: Sea terrace at Firule, east of the centre, looking out over the open channel to the islands.
set.why: Dvor sits on Put Firula, a fifteen-minute walk east of the palace, on a terrace facing the water, so the view is open sea and the islands rather than the port. The kitchen, led in Gault&Millau's 2026 entry by Vesna Vukman, mixes the Mediterranean and the traditional: reviewers keep returning to a ceviche of fish, scampi and scallops in a citrus emulsion, and to a prawn carpaccio. Gault&Millau scores it 16/20.
set.verdict: The sea-terrace night of the three, and the quieter one: you leave the old town behind and eat facing the open water. MICHELIN puts it in its top price bracket, and Gault&Millau ranks it just behind ZOI. It has historically taken a winter break, so it belongs to an October evening, not a December one, unless the house confirms otherwise.

set.hook: Varoš konoba where the day's catch comes to the table on a plate before you choose it.
set.why: Fetivi is the Split word for the true-born locals, and the konoba on Tomića stine works the way its name promises. MICHELIN's inspectors note that the raw catch is carried to each table so you can pick your fish before it goes on the grill. The menu is short and traditional and the prices modest; Gault&Millau's 2026 reviewer singles out a creamy, thick black cuttlefish risotto, and Falstaff adds tuna steak and squid stew.

Choose the fish from the plate, take the black risotto, drink the house white. It is small and popular, so book; and confirm the closing day, because the listings disagree.

set.hook: Small-terrace Varoš konoba on the street it is named after, grilled sardines and local wine until midnight.
set.why: Šperun takes its name from the short street at the edge of Veli Varoš where it stands, at number 3, a few minutes' walk from the Riva. set.hook: Dalmatian classics upstairs in the 15th-century Papalić Palace, above the lanes of the old town.
set.why: You climb from a narrow lane into the 15th-century Papalić Palace, the Gothic townhouse that also holds the city museum, and Apetit occupies an upper floor, quiet above the crowds below. The kitchen keeps to Dalmatian classics, cooked simply with a small twist: pašticada, homemade pasta, and the offal the tourist menus skip, tongue and tripe. Diners also remember the bread and olive oil set down first.
set.verdict: A calm, mid-to-upper-priced lunch inside the palace quarter, good when guests want the old dishes without the street noise. Reviews are mixed on consistency and service, and no guide rates it in 2026, so take it for the room and the pašticada rather than for ambition.
set.caveat: Upper floor, stairs only (floor disputed); no guide rating in 2026

set.hook: Tiny counter kitchen in the palace lanes, menu written each morning from the market; no bookings, cash only.
set.why: Villa Spiza is one small room with a counter and a kitchen squeezed into one side, on Kružićeva inside the palace. Ivana Gamulin, daughter of the Split chef Nikica Gamulin, cooks what she bought that morning at the market and the fish hall, and her sister Nada makes the desserts. The board changes daily, with grilled fish, black risotto and homemade pasta with seafood or mushrooms, and when a dish runs out it is gone.
set.verdict: The best-value plate inside the walls and the one with a queue to prove it: in summer the wait can reach two hours. Come early, bring cash, accept what is on the board. In late autumn the line shortens, but the hours shrink too, so check its social pages on the day.
set.signature: Whatever fish is on the board, then Nada's chocolate cake
set.caveat: No reservations, cash only; winter hours shorter and closed Sundays

set.hook: Glass-fronted wine bistro beside the fish market, open from morning to late, walls lined with bottles.
set.why: Bokeria borrows its name from the market hall of a big Spanish city and sits, fittingly, next to Split's own fish market on Domaldova, just west of the palace. Gault&Millau's 2026 reviewer notes it fills from morning to late at night; diners keep naming the octopus, the risotto, the carpaccio and the sea bass.

set.name: Zinfandel Food & Wine Bistro
set.hook: A MICHELIN-listed wine bistro in a narrow old-town street, about 15 Croatian wines by the glass.
set.why: Zinfandel takes its name from the grape that DNA work traced back to Dalmatia's Tribidrag, and it sits on Marulićeva, a narrow lane off the western edge of the palace. It runs from breakfast to late evening, with live music some nights. The list covers the whole of Croatia with around fifteen wines by the glass, and the kitchen mixes Dalmatian recipes with international plates: pasta in a prošek sauce with prawns, boards of cured meat, cheese and marinated fish.
set.verdict: The most useful glass in the old town now that Paradox is reported closed, and the only wine bar in this guide with a MICHELIN listing in 2026. The food is better than bar snacks, the room is busy and close. Go for a flight of Croatian reds before or after dinner, or make it the dinner itself. Hours vary by source, so call.
set.signature: Pasta with prošek sauce and prawns, with a glass of Tribidrag or Plavac Mali
set.caveat: Hours conflict across sources (some say closed Sunday, some Monday); small room, book at night

set.hook: Small stone tavern just off the palace's north-east corner, Dalmatian pot dishes cooked with a modern hand.
set.why: The name is the Dalmatian word for a slow, rich sauce, and the kitchen lives up to it: Gault&Millau's 2026 reviewer singles out the tećade, the braised pot dishes, alongside the day's fish. The room is a small stone tavern with a terrace on Tolstojeva, a few steps outside the palace walls. Two chefs, Duje Kanajet and Mateo Kordić, cook traditional recipes with precise, current technique, and the wine list stays mostly local.
set.verdict: Not a grand table: a small, well-priced house that cooks the Dalmatian repertoire properly, which is rarer in the centre than it should be. Good for a guest who wants pašticada or a rižot without the tourist-menu version. Reservations are mandatory and the room is small, so it fits a last-minute dinner only if you call early.

set.hook: A small family konoba at the foot of Marjan hill, cooking whatever the fish market had that morning.
set.why: Konoba Marjan is a few tables on Senjska, the stepped street in Veli Varoš that climbs toward the Marjan park. Father, mother and son run it, and they say the menu changes daily with what the nearby fish market has to offer. That shows on the board: cuttlefish brujet, gregada with potato, prawn pasta, black risotto, a whole grilled fish deboned at the table. The wine list leans on small Croatian producers.
set.verdict: A real fish konoba rather than a palace-front trap, and well loved for its grill. It is small, so it fills and the kitchen runs out: one spring 2026 diner found the black risotto gone by 7:30 pm, and others reported slow service on full nights. Book, come early, and order the fish of the day rather than the menu standards.
set.signature: Whole grilled fish of the day, or cuttlefish brujet

set.hook: The takeaway ćevapi window on Matošića: grilled meat in a soft lepinja, onion and ajvar, cash only.
set.why: Kantun Paulina is a corner hatch on Matošića, a lane parallel to Marmontova, with a few stools and a queue. It has been grilling ćevapi for decades, the start date is argued (1967, 1979, or 'over 37 years'), and it does them the Split way: in a thick, doughy lepinja with ajvar, red pepper relish, and raw onion rather than the kajmak of Sarajevo. Portions come small, medium or large.
set.verdict: The quick meal that locals argue about rather than a sit-down, and good value next to anything on the Riva. Reviews in 2025 still put it among the best ćevapi in town, with a few saying it has slipped. Expect a line, bring cash, eat standing or on the move.

set.caveat: Cash only; queues; few seats; no 2026-dated evidence found

set.name: Pazar (Green Market)
set.hook: Split's open-air produce market against the palace's east wall, busiest from dawn to mid-morning.
set.why: Pazar spreads its stalls along the outside of Diocletian's east wall by the Silver Gate, and it is where the city still buys its greens. Family farms (OPG) sell from the central aisles: tomatoes, figs fresh or dried, wild herbs, olive oil, honey, fresh farm cheese at a few euros a kilo next to aged Pag sheep cheese at around 35. The vegetable sellers clear out by early afternoon; at 7 am the best of it is still on the tables.
set.verdict: The place to provision a galley and to see what is in season before choosing a konoba. Go early, carry cash and taste before you buy; the second ring of stalls sells souvenirs and imported fruit. Not a place to eat, but the most honest view of the Dalmatian table in town.
set.signature: Dried figs, Pag cheese and a bottle of local olive oil for the boat
set.caveat: Go before 9:00; stalls thin out by noon; cash

set.name: Ribarnica (Fish Market)
set.hook: The morning fish market off Marmontova, cash on the counter and the best fish gone before nine.
set.why: Locals call it peškarija. The fish hall sits just off Marmontova, a short walk from the sulphur springs of the old spa, and local legend says the sulphur keeps the flies away. The marble counters carry what the boats brought in: whole sea bass and bream, octopus sold by weight, cuttlefish, scampi for the grill, small oily fish for frying. It is a working market; by early afternoon the counters are hosed down.
set.verdict: Go before the konoba lunch to learn what is in season and what it costs before you see it on a menu. Buyers for galleys can deal here directly, in cash. The best whole fish go before 9:00. Do not come after 13:00, and check Sunday before you plan around it.

set.caveat: Cash; best fish go before 9:00; Sunday opening disputed

set.name: Buffet Fife
set.hook: The no-frills Dalmatian canteen on the Matejuška waterfront, open all day, where locals and crews eat cheap.
set.why: Fife sits on Trumbićeva obala facing the little fishermen's harbour at Matejuška, spread over two buildings: a terrace on the waterfront road, a small room inside and a separate dining room. Nothing is dressed up. Plates arrive fast and heavy, the cooking is home Dalmatian, pašticada with gnocchi, fish soup, fried squid, grilled fish, and the tables mix fishermen, students and tour groups. The city's own Advent programme listed a New Year's party here, which tells you who the regulars are.
set.verdict: The honest cheap lunch on the waterfront, not a destination for cooking. Portions are big and prices low by Riva standards, and it is one of the few tables here that seems to trade through the winter. Expect queues at peak times and brisk service. Send the crew, not the guests who want a tablecloth.
set.signature: Pašticada with gnocchi, or fried squid if the pašticada has run out
set.caveat: Queues at peak times; reservations reportedly only for large groups; one reviewer found it cash only
